item.title: A Meeting With Elizabeth Holmes
item.description:
Confidence

A Meeting With Elizabeth Holmes

Confidence and powerful connections can even make experts doubt themselves.

Posted November 4, 2026

Key points
  • Persuasive, well-connected people can make even experts doubt what they know.
  • We tend to trust confident people more, especially when their claims are difficult or costly to check.
  • Healthcare depends on trusting others, which makes it essential to know whom to trust and why.
  • Consider whether their expertise is relevant and provide evidence and independent support for their claims.

Like many Americans, I recently watched You Can See Everything, the documentary that follows Elizabeth Holmes through the weeks before she reported to prison. I left the theater fascinated and bewildered. Throughout the movie, I kept asking the same question the filmmakers seem to be asking: Am I being deceived, or am I missing something because I don't know enough?

I have asked myself that question about Holmes before. In July 2013, I was the Deputy Commissioner for the New York City Health Department, where I oversaw the city's infectious disease programs and the public health laboratory. City Hall asked me to meet with a promising new lab-testing company; a few weeks later, I joined an hour-long video call with Holmes, her team, and our lab director.

Deputy Secretary of Defense and former Secretary of Defense meet Elizabeth Holmes in 2013.
Source: Department of Defense

I still have my notes. Holmes and her colleagues told us that their company, Theranos, had developed a more convenient way to test blood in small amounts that would cut testing costs by 30 percent.

They said:

A wide range of tests had been validated
Federal and New York State regulatory approvals were complete
They secured a Department of Defense contract.
Testing was scheduled to launch at New York Walgreens pharmacies within months.

My colleague and I asked repeatedly about the underlying science and data. Every time, we got the same answer: they could not disclose business secrets, but everything worked and was approved. Rest assured.

When the call ended, my colleague and I were dumbfounded. Nothing we knew about collecting specimens, validating tests, or getting regulatory approval made their story plausible. And yet I doubted myself. Holmes spoke with such composure and certainty and had such powerful connections and investors that I kept wondering: Did she know something about science or lab regulations that I didn't?

We offered to evaluate the device in our lab before any wider use. Neither side ever followed up. When the Wall Street Journal published its first investigation into the company in October 2015, I called my colleague, and we both said the same thing: "We knew it!" Most of what she said in that meeting was not true.

After watching the movie, I kept thinking about that incident and how it raised a hard healthcare problem: knowing when to trust your own expertise and when to defer to someone else's.

Confidence Is Not the Same as Competence

We assume that people who sound certain know more than we do. This is particularly common when checking a person’s claims is difficult or costly. That describes the Theranos meeting almost exactly. We could not check her claims because she said her data was confidential, and she spoke with absolute certainty.

While the lack of data made me suspicious, I fell prey to something known as “the halo effect,” where people with credibility in one domain are often thought to be credible experts in other domains. Theranos had funders and board members who had extremely prestigious backgrounds in government and the military. Even though none of them had a background in laboratory medicine, I assumed they had done sufficient due diligence on the technology.

Can You Be an Expert in Everything?

A big challenge in health: The body is so complex that none of us can be experts in everything. As a physician, if I order an MRI on a patient, I rely on the radiologist to interpret it correctly. When I order a blood test, I rely on laboratory technicians to use validated methods and equipment. I could not do my job if I had to personally verify that everyone knows what they are doing and is doing it correctly. The need to trust others is even greater for patients, because most of them will not be medical experts.

The problem, of course, is that humans are imperfect. Medical errors are, unfortunately, quite common. Someone did something wrong—errors of commission; someone forgot to do something—errors of omission. And, because medical knowledge is always growing, something correct 10 years ago may be incorrect now. I always encourage people to ask their healthcare providers questions and, with major health decisions, to seek second opinions.

How to Decide When to Trust a Health Expert

How do you decide when and whom to trust? Here are a few questions you can ask whether you are a patient talking to a doctor or interpreting health claims online.

First, is this an area where you have real knowledge and experience? If so, give your own judgment more weight than you are inclined to, even when the person across from you is more confident than you are.

Second, does their authority come from the relevant field? A famous name, a large social media following, or impressive business credentials do not mean they understand how a vaccine works or what a blood test measures.

Third, is the other person offering evidence or only certainty? Consider asking, “What is the evidence that supports this approach? Is this what expert guidelines recommend?” Trustworthy experts can explain their reasoning or point you to high-quality studies or published guidelines to check their claims.

Fourth, has anyone independently checked? Has it been approved by the FDA or another government regulatory agency? Or do major professional organizations recommend it?

We need our health experts and institutions to see everything—the methods and the data—to make sure medications, vaccines, and other health interventions are safe and effective. But when someone asks for our trust and won’t back it up with data, we need to consider trusting our own judgment or asking for a second opinion.

item.title: Why Curlews Are the New Canaries in the Coal Mine
item.description:
Environment

Why Curlews Are the New Canaries in the Coal Mine

Our national grasslands may be one of the country’s best-kept secrets.

Posted November 4, 2026

Key points
  • Kumar uses an elegant intelligent shorebird with a rounded body as an indicator of environmental damage.
  • Seeing why grassland birds are in trouble could move us to engage with this stunning ecosystem.
  • Kumar takes readers into the heart of the drama so we can understand what the birds may be experiencing.
Source: Priyanka Kumar.

One would have to be totally out of touch to think that the Earth's diverse ecosystems are healthy and thriving. Numerous habitats are in dire straits, and many nonhuman animal residents are trying to tell us we must act to save everyone.

Grassland animals can tell us what is happening if we would only listen to them, and in her new book titled The Grassland Queen: An Avian Love Story in the American Plains, naturalist, filmmaker, and author Priyanka Kumar does just that by focusing on the lives of long-billed curlews, "an elegant shorebird with a rounded body and an improbably elongated bill—a highly intelligent bird that mates for life." I think of these birds as the proverbial canary in the coal mine, telling us that things where they live aren't going well, and Kumar carefully explains why we must listen to what they are saying.

Marc Bekoff: Why did you write The Grassland Queen?

Priyanka Kumar: As a naturalist and educator at the University of New Mexico, it’s my passion to research birds in the context of their ecosystems. The Grassland Queen shows how a community of birds can grow close to a naturalist’s heart, like they are extended family. Over years of researching curlews in grasslands, I returned to my daily life and found myself wondering how my birds were faring in the blazing fields, with heat radiating from dirt and stone.

The long-billed curlew is admittedly a strange-looking bird, with an impossibly long bill, like a creature out of prehistoric times. Curlew parents are insanely devoted to keeping their chicks safe from predators such as ravens, coyotes, foxes, and Swainson’s hawk. A curlew father is a Shakespearean character, dithering one moment, dive-bombing the next—I saw twists and turns and surprising bursts of drama on my days of fieldwork.

MB: How does your book relate to your background and general areas of interest?

PK: My work as a naturalist is deeply informed by my Himalayan childhood and how I experienced and loved nature as a child. I first wrote about long-billed curlews and a dozen other species in my book, Conversations with Birds. I am grateful that the book continues to resonate with readers and inspires them to deepen their engagement with nature.

Over time, I kept coming back to curlews. I wanted to observe them deeply. Long-billed curlews form lifelong pair bonds; the male and female may winter in different coastal areas, but they miraculously return each summer to the same grassland, find one another, and attempt to raise a family. They’re such relatable birds.

MB: Who do you hope to reach?

PK: Our national grasslands are one of the country’s best-kept secrets—the wildlife is exquisite, from the pronghorns to the burrowing owls. Grasslands have been very generous to humans—more than half of the human diet comes from grasses and their seed heads such as wheat, rice, rye, and oats. It’s time to return the favor and care about how grasslands are changing.

Source: Princeton University Press/with permission.

Grassland birds are in trouble—they’re the fastest-declining group of birds in North America. The ecosystem that the curlews have relied on for so long—they coevolved here with bison—is being relentlessly fragmented by industrial agriculture and development. Even the grasslands that remain are sometimes too degraded to support birds. My narrative about the curlew's life also shows a wider community of underappreciated grassland animals.

MB: What are some of the topics you consider and what are some of your major messages?

PK: It’s a marvel that curlews eke out a living in North American grasslands, which can sometimes look so scorched and bleak. Parts of the Great Plains have been in a megadrought, which means fewer grasshoppers and beetles for curlew chicks. These chicks need to eat, grow, learn to fly, and migrate back to the wetlands—without their parents—over one fraught summer.

It’s critical to understand the bird communities that live in the American Plains and how global warming can unravel ecosystems. After oceans, grasslands are the largest ecosystem on Earth. I take readers into the heart of this unfolding drama so that we can understand what the birds themselves may be experiencing.

MB: What challenge did you face while writing the book?

PK: The hardest part of writing this book was leaving the grasslands and all those lovely birds behind. In one of the last chapters, when I’m in the grasslands, I’m in wildfire smoke. With all the climate stresses, this ecosystem is pretty vulnerable to overheating and out-of-control wildfires.

Eighty percent of American grasslands are private, and we have no concerted national strategy—though there’s broad consensus that we need one—to incentivize private landowners to become more bird-friendly, whether through rotational grazing or creating wild margins at the edges of agricultural fields.

MB: Are you hopeful that as people learn more about this and treat birds with more respect and compassion?

PK: Literature and storytelling catalyze us to empathize with the lives of others. I hope this book pulls readers out of their everyday lives, transports them, and makes them feel affection for long-billed curlews. I’ve felt a sustained love for these birds over more than two decades.

I created an impressionistic painting: If you look closely, you’ll see many dots, which are the field observations. But hopefully, when you step back, you get the sweep of the grand landscape and the dramas playing out among wildlife and between wildlife and humans. This book is about being fiercely present. Will we choose to be present for the birds and the degradation their ecosystems face? It is painful to be present, especially when you find yourself looking for curlews on a shooting range, but there’s also a great joy that sneaks up on you just when you’re about to give up.

item.title: The Powerful Impact of Social Comparisons in Everyday Life
item.description:
Social Comparison Theory

The Powerful Impact of Social Comparisons in Everyday Life

People with similar attributes create the most potent social comparisons.

Posted November 4, 2026

Key points
  • Social comparisons are everywhere and have potent effects on our lives.
  • People who share related attributes feel the most powerful effects.
  • These effects extend to how our children compare with other children.

"Did she do that? Did she do that?" said the mother of my daughter's friend, her eyes wide and her jaw dropped — her entire system in a state of shock.

She had just arrived at the daycare center to pick up her daughter. Near the entrance was a chalkboard where the kids were encouraged to draw unrestricted.

Some minutes earlier, my daughter and her daughter had both been drawing stick figures. I had arrived early, and my daughter had pleaded with me to "draw some people." However, the daycare center had a strict policy against parents helping their kids; kids should develop independence while at the center.

Gently, I reminded her that I wasn't allowed to help, but she persisted. And so after checking that no staff members were watching, I made quick drawings of a couple of kids. They were barely passable, but next to her daughter's stick figures, they were Da Vincis.

I had just returned the chalk to my daughter, who was now busily applying some final touches, when the other girl's mom showed up. The two drawings contrasted sharply, leaving a powerful impression on the mom. But what could I say? I had violated the center's rules.

I had to put the mom out of her misery. Under my breath, I said, "No, no, I drew them. She begged me to do it. Don't tell anyone."

Echoing the two masks of Greek theater, her face shifted from tragedy to a kind of joy.

Tragedy and Comedy
Source: Tim Green/Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0

Why did she feel this comparison so keenly?

A few details explain this. My daughter and her friend were the same age (4) and gender. They also had the same birthday. Similarity in related attributes increases the impact of social comparisons. If her friend were a boy and a year older, the mother might have brushed off the comparison; it lacked relevance. Parents often zero in on attributes for a sense of how a comparison should register, especially at these early ages when a year or more can be especially important in determining achievement.

I often think of this episode. To me, it captures how social comparisons affect people in everyday life.

How we stack up with others often has deciding consequences for success in important areas of life, from work to romance, and for the feelings about self that follow from these outcomes. Part of growing up and maturing as adults is about assessing strengths and weaknesses largely determined by relative standing, grappling with the emotional and practical implications of such assessments, and making life choices guided by this process.

And, of course, our kids are extensions of ourselves.

In my experience, I can think of no better example of these truths than this small but telling incident occurring in my daughter’s pre-school.

item.title: Zinc: The Missing Link in Anorexia?
item.description:
Anorexia Nervosa

Zinc: The Missing Link in Anorexia?

This essential mineral is the keystone in nutritional supplementation for AN.

Posted November 4, 2026

Key points
  • Zinc deficiency looks remarkably like anorexia—and many anorexic patients are deficient in zinc.
  • Zinc is involved in hundreds of biological processes, including appetite regulation.
  • Decades of studies support the use of zinc for anorexia nervosa.
  • Detecting and correcting zinc deficiency is possible.

Over more than three decades of treating children, adolescents, and adults with eating disorders—including anorexia nervosa—I’ve seen the same pattern again and again. A patient arrives with severe anorexia, and they turn out to be severely deficient in one essential mineral: zinc.

So, while anorexia is a complicated disease, one part of treatment is very simple: If you, your child, or your patient has anorexia, the first and best step toward recovery may be correcting a zinc deficiency.

Source: vadimguzhva / Stock photo ID:1014887888

Three Crucial Links Between Zinc and Anorexia

1: Zinc deficiency looks remarkably like anorexia. Imagine I described someone with a poor appetite, weight loss, slowed growth, changes in taste and smell, depression, anxiety, problems concentrating, low energy, social withdrawal, and digestive complaints. Would you think I was describing anorexia nervosa? You’d be right.

But I’d also be describing the symptoms of…zinc deficiency. Yes, many of the hallmark symptoms of anorexia are also classic symptoms of zinc deficiency. That doesn’t prove zinc deficiency causes anorexia. But it raises an obvious question: Could at least some of what we’ve traditionally thought of as the symptoms of anorexia actually be driven—or made worse—by a deficiency of this one nutrient?

2: Zinc deficiency is extremely common in people with anorexia. When researchers measure zinc levels in people with anorexia, they consistently find that a substantial percentage are deficient. Depending on the study and the methods used, at least half—and in some studies many more—show evidence of inadequate zinc status.

3: Remove zinc from an animal’s diet—and it begins to resemble someone with anorexia. In several studies, when scientists fed laboratory animals a diet lacking zinc, the animals ate less and lost weight. Growth slowed. They became less active socially. Females stopped reproducing. In short, they displayed features of anorexia nervosa.

Source: piotr_malczyk / Stock photo ID:2206056066

Why Zinc Is So Important

Zinc is involved in hundreds of biological processes throughout the body; it helps regulate the activity of more than 300 enzymes, and it influences thousands of proteins that control growth, repair, metabolism, and communication between cells. In terms of our understanding of anorexia, zinc is crucial for:

Appetite regulation. Zinc participates in the complex network of hormones and signaling molecules that help regulate hunger, satiety, and energy balance. When zinc levels fall, that finely tuned system begins to malfunction. Appetite often declines. Food becomes less appealing. Eating can begin to feel like an obligation rather than a pleasure. This creates a cruel biological cycle.

A person who is already eating too little develops a zinc deficiency. The zinc deficiency further suppresses appetite. Reduced appetite leads to even less food intake. That, in turn, worsens the zinc deficiency.

I’ve seen this cycle happen so many times that I now think of it as one of the central biological engines driving anorexia. Breaking this cycle is one of the reasons correcting zinc deficiency can be so important.

Intra-brain communication. Zinc helps regulate the activity of several neurotransmitter systems that have long been implicated in anorexia, including glutamate and GABA, while also influencing serotonin and other chemical messengers involved in mood and anxiety.

The Scientific Evidence for Zinc

You may be thinking: The biological connection between zinc deficiency and anorexia certainly sounds convincing. But does correcting the deficiency actually help people recover?

For more than four decades, studies on zinc and anorexia point in the same general direction: When people with anorexia receive supplemental zinc, they tend to improve. They gain weight more readily. Their appetite and sense of taste may return. Their mood becomes more stable. Physical development resumes. And, importantly, zinc has generally proved safe and well-tolerated.

One of the most impressive clinical trials enrolled 35 women who had been hospitalized with anorexia. Each patient was randomly assigned to receive either 100 milligrams (mg) of zinc daily or a placebo. The women continued taking zinc or a placebo until they achieved a 10% increase in body mass index (BMI). The results were striking.

The women receiving zinc increased their BMI at twice the rate of those receiving the placebo. Think about what that means. Both groups were hospitalized. Both were receiving expert care for anorexia. Both were working to regain weight. The principal difference between the two groups was that one also received zinc. And that group recovered significantly faster.

Writing in The International Journal of Eating Disorders, the researchers concluded, ‘‘The use of zinc supplementation should be considered in the treatment of AN patients.’’ I agree.

You’ll find citations to many other similarly impressive studies in the references at the end of this blog. The overall message from the research is that correcting zinc deficiency can improve recovery from anorexia nervosa.

Discovering Zinc Deficiency

Unlike vitamin C or niacin deficiency, zinc deficiency doesn’t cause one distinct, readily diagnosable disease. Instead, it can produce a wide and seemingly unrelated assortment of physical and psychological problems. These can include:

  • loss of appetite
  • changes in taste and smell
  • weight loss
  • poor resistance to infection
  • slow wound healing
  • delayed growth or sexual maturation
  • apathy
  • anxiety
  • depression

To complicate matters, normal blood zinc does not always mean normal zinc status—because only a tiny fraction of the body’s zinc circulates freely in the blood, and the body works hard to maintain adequate zinc in the bloodstream.

For these reasons, laboratory results must be interpreted in context. A zinc value near the lower end of the reference range may be particularly significant when it appears alongside anorexia, restrictive eating, poor appetite, altered taste, slow healing, frequent infection, anxiety, depression, or other signs associated with deficiency.

Source: Lacheev / Stock photo ID:2215926591

Achieving Optimal Zinc Levels

Once zinc deficiency has been identified—or is strongly suspected—the next step is correcting it. I generally recommend beginning with therapeutic doses as part of a comprehensive program of targeted nutritional therapy. My protocols are the following:

For adolescents, the typical starting dose is 15 mg of zinc twice daily, for a daily total of 30 mg.

For adults, the typical starting dose is 30 mg twice daily, for a daily total of 60 mg.

After approximately three months, these doses are generally reduced by half—to 15 mg daily for adolescents, and 30 mg daily for adults. This level establishes ongoing maintenance of zinc levels during recovery.

These recommendations should be individualized for the patient. The protocol should also be supervised by a qualified healthcare professional knowledgeable about nutritional medicine.

You can read much more about zinc and anorexia in my new book, Finally Nourished: A Science-Based Plan to Correct Malnutrition in Anorexia Nervosa—and Achieve True and Lasting Recovery.

item.title: The Mental Edge: 6 Tools to Use to Perform Better at Anything
item.description:
Coaching

The Mental Edge: 6 Tools to Use to Perform Better at Anything

Practical skills to improve performance, overcome setbacks, and achieve goals.

Posted November 4, 2026

Key points
  • Mental skills need regular practice to become reliable tools under pressure.
  • Reframing replaces catastrophic thoughts with realistic, useful ones.
  • Instructional self-talk guides execution; motivational self-talk builds confidence and drive.
  • Mental rehearsal engages processes similar to physical practice and can improve technical skills.

Mental skills, also called psychological skills, are those mental abilities that allow us to do everything from getting up off the couch, getting through a rough day, managing a pressurized situation, and realizing our potential. These can be learned and honed to meet our individualized needs, and with practice, facilitate both small and large changes in our everyday and game time performance.

Want to be more motivated? Want to learn to handle stress better? Want to improve your run times? Want to start exercising? Want to do better on tests? Want more confidence? You get the idea. These skills can help.

Some foundational mental skills for performance optimization are deep breathing, relaxation skills, self-talk, a reset routine, cognitive reframing, and visualization/imagery.

Motivational self-talk is one example of a key mental skill that helps us achieve our potential.
Source: Brett Jordan/Pexels

Deep Breathing

Deep breathing is a foundational mental skill to incorporate into your mental skills playbook. Deep breathing is key to physical health, mental health, pain management, stress management, emotional control, and cognitive focus in high-stakes situations. Regularly practicing deep breathing is key to being able to use it during challenging moments to refocus and gain control of your physiological response.

Relaxation Skills

There is a wide array of relaxation skills, but three effective ones are deep breathing, specifically diaphragmatic breathing, progressive muscle relaxation, and meditation. Relaxation techniques decrease stress and improve stress tolerance and improve health and cognitive performance.

Self-Talk

For getting motivated, staying focused, and accomplishing goals, there is nothing quite like self-talk. That running dialogue in our heads is extremely powerful and feeds our self-confidence, attentional focus, problem solving abilities, and ability to stick with things even when they are hard. Instructional self-talk gives us the edge we need to remember how to execute complex problems or learn a new skill. If you have ever learned the breaststroke for example, you repeated the instructional mantra “pull, breathe, kick, glide” to yourself many times. Motivational self-talk, on the other, fuels our confidence, focus, and drive. “You got this!”

Reset Routine

When we make a mistake or get thrown off our game by an external variable, sometimes we allow ourselves to be derailed. Performance suffers; we lose focus and become less effective. With a conscious reset routine at the ready to intervene, it is possible to rebound quickly and effectively. A good reset routine is short and incorporates an acknowledgment of the mistake or issue without judgment, a slow, deep breath, and a quick instructional self-talk cue to get back on track. For example, a flight student who has made a mistake during a training flight might 1) acknowledge the mistake without judgment, 2) take a deep 5-7 breath (inhale slowly for 5 counts, exhale slowly for 7 counts), and 3) refocus with the instructional self-talk cue, “Run the next checklist.” After a mistake on the field, an athlete might 1) acknowledge the mistake without judgement, 2) take a slow, deep breath, and 3) refocus with “Next play.”

Cognitive Reframing

Cognitive reframing involves recognizing maladaptive/self-defeating thoughts, examining them objectively, and reframing/replacing them with a realistic and practical thought. The goal here is not unrealistic positivity, but useful and task-focused language. For example, after a mistake during flight training, a student might think “I’m terrible, I’m going to fail out.” This thought is defeatist, absolute, and catastrophic. After examining the thoughts objectively, replacements might be: “I made a common mistake and need to refocus my study time on this area. I’ve worked hard to get here and otherwise I am doing well.” Cognitive reframing or restructuring has been shown to reduce self-critical rumination, increase positive affect, and decrease negative affect in athletes. Cognitive reframing can be used in the moment and is a valuable strategy to move forward after a setback.

Visualization/Imagery

Visualization and imagery are techniques in which we mentally simulate a task (e.g., emergency procedures or a golf swing) in order to better execute that task when needed. Mental rehearsal stimulates neurocognitive processes in much the same way as actually engaging in the activity. Visualization has been shown to enhance mental control, improve motor skills/technical skills and increase self-confidence, and can be used alone or in conjunction with other training strategies. Visualization, imagery, and mental rehearsal are key components of elite performers, including the Navy’s Blue Angels, who routinely engage in chair flying, in which maneuvers are mentally practiced in conjunction with motor movements (see The Blue Angels documentary, 2024, produced by Amazon MGM Studios).

Benefits of mental skills are that they are free, accessible to everyone, and have high levels of effectiveness, which can be applied to virtually any aspect of life. Whether your goal is to manage everyday stress, build confidence, bounce back from setbacks, earn your wings, win a championship, or perform at your best when it matters most, these skills can make a meaningful difference. Like physical skills, mental skills require practice to become effective and readily available when you need them. Start small, choose a skill or two that fits your needs, and practice consistently. Over time, you’ll build a mental skills playbook that you can make work for you.

item.title: The Hidden Dynamics Shaping Our Relationships
item.description:
Relationships

The Hidden Dynamics Shaping Our Relationships

How to turn feedback loops into forward motion.

Posted November 4, 2026

Key points
  • Our thoughts, feelings, and behaviors are shaped by the relationships and environments around us.
  • Feedback loops can reinforce negative relationship patterns or encourage healthier interactions.
  • Changing even one response can interrupt a familiar cycle of frustration or conflict.
  • Systems thinking helps us recognize the hidden dynamics shaping our relationships.

In the words often attributed to the Buddha, “Nothing ever exists entirely alone; everything is in relation to everything else.”

Consider a tree. It can only grow by drawing nutrients from the soil below while relying on rain and sunlight from above. Its roots interact with fungi and microorganisms underground, while its branches provide shelter and nourishment for other living things.

We humans are no different. Our thoughts, feelings, and behaviors don't exist in isolation. They are continually shaped by our relationships and environments. In turn, our own actions, words, tone of voice, and body language influence the people around us, often in ways we don't immediately recognize.

Understanding this interconnectedness is a core competency of spiritual intelligence. [i] It also offers a practical way to understand why we sometimes find ourselves repeating the same frustrating patterns in our relationships, families, and everyday lives.

The Hidden Patterns That Shape Our Lives

My appreciation for systems thinking began during my junior year at MIT in a class taught by organizational theorist Peter Senge.[ii]

Systems thinking invites us to look beyond individual events and recognize the larger networks of relationships in which they occur.[iii] Every action produces reactions elsewhere, and those reactions feed back into the system again. Of course, we only discussed this framework in the context of business, operations, and leadership, but I was immediately struck by how much this perspective explained about human behavior on the whole.

I see it all the time in the couples I counsel. One partner feels unheard and raises their voice in frustration. The other gets defensive and withdraws, protecting themselves. That withdrawal makes the first partner feel more ignored, so they try even harder and more forcefully to break through the "wall," only perpetuating the cycle. From either person's perspective, the problem may appear to be the other's behavior. But when we look at the relationship as a system, we begin to see something different: each person's response is influencing the other's, creating a loop that neither necessarily intends.

It made sense to me to learn that such system dynamics and feedback loops are the heart of several attachment-based couples therapy modalities such as Psychobiological Approach to Couple Therapy (PACT)[iv] and Emotionally Focused Therapy (EFT)[v].

How Feedback Loops Keep Us Stuck, or Help Us Grow

At the heart of systems thinking are two fundamental dynamics: positive and negative feedback loops. Despite their names, positive and negative don't necessarily mean good or bad.

Negative feedback loops stabilize a system, like a thermostat adjusting the temperature in a room. Positive feedback loops, meanwhile, reinforce existing patterns, whether healthy or unhealthy. Appreciation can breed more appreciation, just as frustration can breed more frustration.

Consider what happens when someone close to you expresses genuine appreciation for something you've done. You feel seen and valued, which may inspire you to be more generous or attentive in return. Your response makes the other person feel appreciated, too.

Unfortunately, the reverse is equally possible. Imagine walking into the kitchen and seeing that your partner has left dirty dishes all over the counter. You gripe, "Why do you always leave your dishes for me to clean?" Formulated as a question, through a frustrated tone of voice, this statement is likely to be interpreted by your partner as a criticism. They get defensive and a fight ensues. Alternatively, a more authentic and vulnerable response might sound like, "I am feeling exhausted and disconnected, and I need your help in keeping our space clean. Would you be willing to put your dishes in the dishwasher when done?”

These patterns can become so familiar that we stop noticing them. We begin to see our partner as defensive, or intrusive, our child as difficult, or our friend as inconsiderate, without recognizing how our own reactions may be contributing to the very behaviors that frustrate us.

Changing the Cycle Starts with Awareness

One of the most powerful lessons of systems thinking is that changing even one part of a system can alter the entire dynamic.

Suppose your child is struggling with schoolwork. Your frequent reminders to study could feel like pressure, making them more resistant, and their procrastination will only increase your frustration. Instead of pushing harder, you might ask what's making the work difficult. Responding with curiosity rather than frustration can help break the cycle.

This is where spiritual intelligence becomes especially valuable. Understanding our interconnectedness and interdependence, along with qualities such as self-awareness, compassion, humility, and presence, can help us recognize our automatic reactions and choose how we want to respond.

Try Mapping Your Own Relationships

A useful exercise is to map the feedback loops operating in one of your important relationships.

Think of a recurring interaction, particularly one that leaves you feeling frustrated or misunderstood, and ask yourself:

  1. What typically triggers this interaction?
  2. How do I usually feel and respond?
  3. How does the other person react to my response?
  4. How does their reaction affect my behavior?
  5. What might happen if I responded differently?

Try approaching these questions with curiosity rather than blame. We’re not looking to accuse; we’re looking to diagnose and understand the system at play.

You can also examine relationships where you feel particularly supported. What patterns of behavior make those relationships work, and how might you recreate them elsewhere?

Seeing the Whole System

Systems thinking reminds us that every interaction contributes, however subtly, to the conditions in which our relationships develop. Something as simple as a moment of patience can interrupt a familiar cycle of conflict and create room for a different response.

We may not be able to control how others behave, but we can become more conscious of what we contribute to the systems we share. And sometimes, that small change is enough to set something much larger in motion.

item.title: When Stress Drives Us to the Bathroom
item.description:
Gut-Brain Axis

When Stress Drives Us to the Bathroom

Stress, and the anxiety it provokes, can do a number on your gut.

Posted November 4, 2026

Key points
  • Stress can cause anxiety, which your brain interprets as danger.
  • Anxiety triggers the flight-or-fight response, even if it’s not appropriate.
  • The cycle can lead to strong peristalsis for two evolutionary reasons.

“I have a new philosophy. I'm only going to dread one day at a time.” —Charles Schulz

Stress can drive many people to the bathroom. That stress can come in the form of an overbearing boss, an abusive partner, or just bad news. These people are wired to redirect stress to their gut, and more specifically, defecation. Welcome to anxiety poop.

Just seeing something stressful can make many of us nauseated. You don’t need to actually ride a rickety roller coaster; just looking at it can provide a frisson of anxiety.

You may think you don’t have this issue, but everyone has a strong gut-brain connection. Before a presentation, we get butterflies in our stomach. When we have to make quick decisions under stress, we defer to our gut feelings. When we have to do something difficult, it can be gut-wrenching.

But how is the brain connected to the gut?

Source: midjourney

The gut-brain axis

Anxiety poop is a great example of the gut-brain axis at work. Stress, whether caused by the outside environment or internal microbes, causes serotonin to be released in the gut. That induces peristalsis and an urge to find a bathroom STAT. Not fun, but also not uncommon.

Dialed up high enough, anxiety puts out an all-points bulletin to the body. It affects the fight-or-flight response (sympathetic), as well as the rest-and-digest response (parasympathetic).

The sympathetic fight-or-flight response is wired to the brain via spinal nerves. When triggered, we produce adrenalin and cortisol — the stress drugs — which push us to hulk out, either to fight or run.

Meanwhile, the parasympathetic rest-and-digest system is wired to the brain by the vagus nerve. When this response is triggered, special cells lining the gut secrete serotonin.

We typically think of serotonin as a chemical messenger in the brain. That’s what SSRIs target. But 90% of your serotonin is in your gut, and it doesn’t act like an antidepressant. Instead, it’s in charge of peristalsis, the rhythmic constrictions that pulse your food through the gut. Under stress, a lot of serotonin is released, pulsing your food with a vengeance.

Evolution is frugal

Why has evolution fashioned such behavior?

There are two good reasons: One is the need for speed. If a tiger starts to chase you, you drop what you’re holding and run. For some extra weight loss, your body uses the serotonin technique to evacuate your bowels, making you lighter on your feet. Embarrassment can come later, if you survive the tiger. As a bonus, the energy you would have spent on digestion is now available for sprinting.

This is great for dealing with tigers, but less-than-suitable for menacing bosses or spouses. Constantly being in this state of hypervigilance can damage your gut lining, especially since the fight-or-flight response has usurped all the blood meant for the gut.

The second evolutionary reason is because your anxiety circuits have been repurposed for food poisoning. You have cells in your gut that can detect an invasion by pathogens. They communicate this info to the brain which decides, based on the strength of the signal, whether to purge or not. It tends to err on the dramatic side, and a severe bout of food poisoning will cause speedy evacuation from both ends of the digestive tract.

These two signals of stress—one from the outside and one from the inside—are handled by the same brain circuits. Nature is frugal, and she loves to repurpose anatomy. One way or another, anxiety is going to disrupt your gut.

That makes this circuitry cyclic: A disturbed gut can create anxiety, and anxiety can disturb the gut. This can lead to chronic conditions like IBS, Crohn’s, IBD, and gastric reflux. Over time, it can snowball into systemic inflammation, threatening the health of all your other organs.

Your leverage against stress

This vicious cycle can be tamed, however, into a virtuous cycle. There are some do’s and some don’ts:

Don’t:

  • Eat too much sugar. Sugar can upend microbial populations, favoring pathogens.
  • Drink too much alcohol. Sadly, alcohol affects microbes, your liver, and the integrity of your gut lining.
  • Sit all day. Get up on a regular basis to move your lymph. It stagnates when you sit and can’t sweep up toxins and pathogens as well. Take a walk outside.
  • Take unnecessary antibiotics. Antibiotics kill pathogenic microbes, but most of them also kill the good guys that live in your gut. It can take months to restore them.

Do:

  • Eat fiber like beans, onions, artichokes, asparagus, and berries. Fiber feeds the good microbes in your gut, producing factors that improve cognition, memory, and mood. Start slowly to avoid gas and talk to your doctor if you have any inflammatory gut issues.
  • Eat ferments like yogurt, sauerkraut, kimchi, and kombucha. They are a combination of fiber and probiotics, a double hit of goodness for your gut. (Same caveats here as above.)
  • Get daily exercise, which improves blood flow and helps heal your gut lining.
  • Get good sleep. Both you and your microbes work best when you observe circadian rhythms to sleep at night and be alert during the day.
  • Try to lower your stress at home and at work. Yes, this can be hard.

We have little control over our external stress, although some people find meditating can help them deal with a crazy world. But we have plenty of control over our diet and exercise.

It can be hard to break habits—who wants to voluntarily quit candy or cocktails?—but the payoff is surprisingly large. Once your microbiome is happy, it becomes harder to perturb. A healthy gut can fend off pathogens better than your immune system can. That builds resilience and lowers your natural anxiety.

And all of that can keep you from pooping your pants under stress. So give it a try.

item.title: The Law of Reversed Effort
item.description:
Sleep

The Law of Reversed Effort

Why trying harder can make certain outcomes even harder to achieve

Posted November 4, 2026

Key points
  • The law of reversed effort explains why overthinking can become its own obstacle.
  • Sometimes the highest-leverage move is to stop monitoring whether something is working.
  • We can control our actions, but trying to force an internal state often backfires.
  • Creating the right conditions may work better than pushing harder for the result.

For the better part of this decade, I suffered from a severe case of insomnia. Initially, it had biological origins. After coming down with COVID early in the pandemic, the virus triggered a rare autoimmune condition in me called Morvan syndrome. Morvan’s gift to its victims is profound, treatment-resistant insomnia (agrypnia excitata), and the syndrome can be fatal in up to 20 percent of reported cases. Fortunately (though it’s hard to diagnose), once it’s identified, it’s quite treatable. Unfortunately, prolonged insomnia can develop a learned psychological component, even after the original biological problem improves, so my sleepless nights continued even after IVIG immunotherapy resolved most of the other consequences of the condition.

So, as behavioral scientists often do, I was determined to solve my problem through intellect and science. I bought an Oura Ring and started tracking my sleep. I learned everything I could about sleep hygiene. I hired a sleep coach, therapist, and hypnotherapist. I got a silly pair of glasses and bought all the supplements. I even started injecting myself with peptides purported to help with sleep. Like so many who suffer from insomnia, I just wanted out of it. I jumped the shark when I bought a machine to freeze my prefrontal cortex, a machine so loud my poor wife was now not able to sleep either.

After more than five years of suffering, one little trick made it stop: I decided to stop caring. To be clear, I didn’t suddenly abandon my healthy sleep habits; I just stopped treating good sleep as something I needed to achieve.

The Law of Reversed Effort

If you follow my work, you know Alan Watts has been a significant influence in what I do. Although the law of reversed effort didn’t originate with him, he helped popularize similar ideas through his writing about Taoism and effortless action. Watts even described Lao-tzu as a master of the law of reversed effort.

Despite the name, the law of reversed effort is not a scientific law per se, in the same sense as something found in empirical disciplines. Rather, it’s a psychological idea that there are certain outcomes where increasing conscious effort begins to work against us. Sleep has emerged as the textbook example of this concept, but it shows up in a lot of places. For instance, the paradox of hedonism is the idea that the best way to become unhappy is to chase happiness (the foundation of my book, The Fun Habit). Or the ironic monitoring process, a topic extensively explored by psychologist Daniel Wegner, where in the pursuit of peace of mind, you inadvertently train yourself to subconsciously always scan for threats, therefore making peace of mind elusive.

Why Trying Harder Can Backfire

Here’s how Wegner explains the monitoring process: When we deliberately try to create or suppress a mental state, two processes get activated. One tries to produce the outcome we want; the other monitors whether we are succeeding. Unfortunately, that monitoring process must keep looking for evidence of failure. For instance, if your goal is to stop feeling anxious, some part of your attention must continually ask, “Am I still anxious?”

In my case, with the goal of desperately wanting to fall asleep, my brain (unintentionally) was trained to keep noticing whether I was still awake. In fact, there’s even a sleep treatment that uses this paradox and reverses it. “Paradoxical intention” asks people with insomnia to let go of the effort to force sleep and, in some versions, gently try to stay awake instead. A systematic review and meta-analysis found that paradoxical intention improved important insomnia outcomes and reduced sleep-related performance anxiety (although the authors acknowledged that stronger research in this area is still needed).

When Optimization Becomes the Problem

For those of us like me who enjoy living in health metrics and data, optimization runs the risk of making problems worse. With sleep trackers now becoming ubiquitous, the problem has become so prevalent that researchers now have a term for it: orthosomnia. But hyperfocusing on a personal problem is hardly unique to sleep.

Both of my parents were professors who lived through the publish-or-perish era. Now that I better understand the pressures of that time, I’ve forgiven them for never being around. However, because there is a lot of residual pain from their absence, I’ve always felt a sense of duty to ensure that my children have all the access to me they need.

So, I read all the good parenting books and followed all the parenting influencers on social media; I tried to be the best parent I could be at every step. But beneath all those good intentions, a practice of rumination and a small “sub-agent of evaluation” began to emerge, framing our interactions as performative. In other words, every interaction with my kids was also an opportunity to collect data. Did I handle that correctly? Was I present enough? And even though I hate to admit this one: Do they like me?

Serendipitously, when my sleep miraculously improved, it dawned on me pretty quickly that I could apply the law of reversed effort to other areas of my life. So, I stopped worrying about being a good father (important to note, I didn’t stop being a good father). I was able to pull this off because I benefited from the confidence of knowing I had enough reps in to trust that the one-off disagreements and difficult afternoons were not a referendum. And once I stopped keeping score, something magical happened: I became more available to what was actually happening. The result is we all started having a lot more fun.

The Law of Reversed Effort
Source: Photocreo / depositphotos

Effort Is Not the Enemy

I can already see fans of Ryan Holiday’s work roll their eyes, so let me state the obvious: The law of reversed effort can be problematic if taken too far.

Folks who truly know me understand that my argument is never for passivity or living a life of whimsy. On the contrary, direct effort works well for countless things. If you want to become stronger, you need to lift weights. If you want to learn a musical instrument, you need to practice. If you want deeper relationships, you need to put in the time.

The important distinction to be aware of is between actions we can perform and states we’re trying to force, as well as becoming comfortable with not being wedded to an outcome. I can create a supportive environment in which to go to bed. I cannot command myself to sleep. I can listen carefully and be present with my children. I cannot force them to be endearing at every turn. I can flex my agency and autonomy to create time for enjoyable experiences. I can only order myself to become happy at my own peril.

Create the Conditions, Then Get Out of the Way

Here’s a question I find myself asking more and more these days: Is this something I can directly affect? Or is this something more likely to emerge if I create the right conditions?

If you’ve gotten this far, I hope you see it was never about caring less. It’s about recognizing when your level of caring has quietly turned into an anxiety trap, because you’re trying to control something that is uncontrollable.

Some things respond beautifully when we push harder. Others seem to require us to create the right conditions, loosen our grip, and then simply allow them to happen. Learning this hasn’t just helped me improve my sleep. It’s made my life better by freeing up energy to be fully present with those I love and cherish. I’m excited to see where else I can benefit from the law of reversed effort as I apply it to other areas of my life. Stay tuned.

item.title: It's So Much More Than Used Clothing
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

It's So Much More Than Used Clothing

What Goodwill showed me about disability, accommodations, and employment.

Posted November 4, 2026

Key points
  • Goodwill is the largest employer of persons with disabilities in Florida.
  • People with disabilities are unemployed at roughly twice the rate of other workers.
  • Accommodations and employee training are a cost effective ways of expanding the workforce.
Making pants for the army
Source: Eva Ritvo/Used with permission

When I thought of Goodwill, I pictured used clothing. Then I toured its Miami-Dade facility and learned so much more.

Goodwill Industries of South Florida helps people with disabilities and other employment barriers gain greater independence through job training, employment, and placement services. According to president and CEO David Landsberg, it is Florida’s largest employer of people with disabilities and the 18th-largest employer in South Florida.

Its businesses include manufacturing military and other apparel, providing custodial services to federal workplaces, and operating a commercial laundry. They also provide career training in fields such as HVAC and solar installation and place graduates in community positions.

I was particularly moved by the employees making American flags for veterans’ burials. These flags will cover caskets for our veterans. I watched a blind man sew with remarkable precision and speed.

I saw enthusiasm and pride throughout the tour, especially during a Spirit of Goodwill Band rehearsal. The musicians, who work at Goodwill and have a variety of disabilities, were superb. They are given time during the workweek to practice, and they perform at community functions, including the organization’s fundraising gala.

Why Work Matters

Many of us carry disability insurance in case illness or injury prevents us from working. But what about someone born with a disability, or who developed one in childhood, who has never had the opportunity to work?

The World Health Organization’s 2022 guidelines recognize meaningful work as a source of confidence, accomplishment, and inclusion. Work gives our days structure, with tasks to complete and opportunities to grow. A conversation over lunch or someone asking how our weekend went may seem trivial until those interactions are missing, as many of us discovered during the pandemic.

As a parent who has spent decades advocating for my daughter and worrying about her future, I know how deeply reassuring it is to see an adult child take on work responsibilities and form relationships outside the family.

Finding meaning at work
Source: Patrice Samara/Used with permission

Too Many People Are Still Left Out

The Americans with Disabilities Act protects equal opportunity among qualified people with disabilities. Employers with 15 or more employees should not discriminate and should provide reasonable accommodations if the applicant can meet the job's qualifications. Yet, too many are unemployed.

According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, in 2025, the unemployment rate among people with disabilities ages 16 and older was 8.3 percent, compared with 4.1 percent among those without disabilities. Among people ages 16 to 64 with a disability, just 41.8 percent were working or looking for work in 2025.

Eileen Grubba, a disability activist, award-winning actress, writer, and producer, shared with me her valuable perspective: “Those with disabilities often have the most to offer. They have survived the unthinkable. We rarely consider what they handle every single day, and what they’ve learned because of it. We need to open our minds and turn to those who know best how to adapt, adjust, and overcome, simply because they’ve been overcoming all their lives."

Seeing Potential

Goodwill’s founder, Edgar J. Helms, expressed the organization’s guiding idea: “Not charity, but a chance.”

I left the tour thinking how little I knew about workplace accommodations and how heartwarming it is to see others succeed.

You might contact your local Goodwill or another employment organization and ask whether you can visit. A lot can be achieved through training, time, and connection.

Making a flag
Source: Eva Ritvo Used with permission

item.title: The Value of Appreciation
item.description:
Positive Psychology

The Value of Appreciation

How to get more awe from ordinary days

Posted November 4, 2026

Key points
  • Recognizing the value in small, ordinary moments may increase psychological wealth.
  • Research links greater appreciation of the everyday with greater life satisfaction.
  • Everyday experiences can offer opportunities for awe when approached with curiosity and wonder.

Which is worth more: a million dollars today or a penny that doubles each day for 30 days?

At first, the million looks like the obvious choice.

The penny begins at one cent on day one and doubles each day afterward. By day 10, the balance is a measly $5.12. By day 20, the balance reaches a meager $5,242.88. By day 30, it reaches $5,368,709.12, more than five times the lump sum.

That is the power of compounding. Small beginnings can be easy to underestimate; early progress can look almost insignificant.

Everyday life also offers valuable moments that are easy to overlook: a small gesture of kindness, a moment of connection worth savoring, a heartfelt moment of gratitude.

Source: Henderson / Unsplash

These are psychological pennies: small acts of appreciation that are easy to take for granted but are worth repeating in pursuit of the good life. The invitation is to make appreciation a regular practice, rather than reserve it for one extraordinary occasion.

What people usually think of as extraordinary is not likely to happen every day. Small reasons for gratitude offer more frequent opportunities to experience the benefits of appreciation. Waiting for something extraordinary can lead people to overlook the value already present in their lives.

Appreciation Has Two Complementary Meanings

Psychologists Mitchel Adler and Nancy Fagley define appreciation as “acknowledging the value and meaning of something—an event, a person, a behavior, an object—and feeling a positive emotional connection to it.” They identify eight aspects of appreciation, including gratitude, appreciation of the present moment, and awe.

In finance, appreciation means an increase in value. A home or stock portfolio appreciates when its price rises.

The connection is a useful metaphor for psychological wealth. Recognizing value can increase the value people experience. An ordinary conversation with a friend can feel richer when someone recognizes the gift of having that person in their life. An ordinary afternoon can feel extraordinary when a person pauses to appreciate being alive and the opportunity to spend time with someone they love. In this sense, recognizing the value already present in relationships and experiences can increase how rich life feels.

Source: Sebastian Pichler / Unsplash

Finding Awe

In a 2012 study of 243 participants, psychologist Nancy Fagley found that appreciation was associated with greater life satisfaction. Awe offers one way to practice appreciation in ordinary life. Awe involves a sense of vastness that challenges a person’s usual understanding of the world.

A person does not necessarily need to visit the Grand Canyon or the Himalayas to experience awe. Someone might pause to consider the complexity of a living tree, witness an act of kindness, or feel a profound sense of wonder at a heart that keeps beating without conscious instruction.

In a small randomized study, psychologist Virginia Sturm and colleagues asked adults to take weekly 15-minute outdoor walks for eight weeks. One group also received instructions to approach their surroundings with wonder and seek out novelty. Compared with the control group, which received the walking assignment without those additional instructions, those encouraged to seek wonder and novelty reported greater increases over time in daily positive emotions involving connection with others.

Three Psychological Pennies to Invest Today

To practice appreciation more consistently, choose a familiar activity and consider a more appreciative lens through which to view it.

Give one person your full attention. During a conversation with a friend or loved one, set aside distractions and appreciate the opportunity to spend time together. Listen with interest. When appropriate, let them know you are glad to have them in your life.

Source: Brooke Lark / Unsplash

Reconsider something familiar. During a routine moment, notice something that is easy to take for granted. At a meal, that might be the nourishment the food provides, the people who made the meal possible, or the pleasure of tasting something you enjoy.

Take a walk with curiosity. During a walk, look closely at something you would usually pass by. Consider the complexity of a living tree, for example, or the scale of the sky above it. Allow time for curiosity and wonder.

The penny that began at one cent reaches $5.37 million by day 30. Psychological pennies can be just as easy to overlook, and compounding them over time may increase your psychological wealth. Small, ordinary moments can be worth doubling down on. Recognizing the value already present in such moments can increase how rich life feels.

The practical idea is to return to such moments throughout the day and appreciate them more fully, rather than postpone appreciation until something extraordinary happens. There is no guaranteed rate of return in life satisfaction, but there are good reasons to invest consistently over the long run.

Those are investments that can be made today, and made again tomorrow.
